{{short description|Quartic plane curve}}
[[Image:LimaçonTrisectrix.svg|right|thumb|300px|The limaçon trisectrix specified as the polar equation <math>r=a(1+2\cos\theta),</math> where {{math|''a'' > 0}}. When {{math|''a'' < 0}}, the resulting curve is the reflection of this curve with respect to the line <math>\theta=\pi/2.</math> As a function, {{mvar|r}} has a period of {{math|2π}}. The inner and outer loops of the curve intersect at the pole.]]

{{main|Limaçon}}

In [[geometry]], a '''limaçon trisectrix''' is the name for the  [[quartic plane curve]] that is a [[trisectrix]] that is specified as a [[limaçon]].  The shape of the limaçon trisectrix can be specified by other curves particularly as a [[rose (mathematics)|rose]], [[conchoid (mathematics)|conchoid]] or [[epitrochoid]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Trisectrix |author=Xah Lee |url=http://xahlee.info/SpecialPlaneCurves_dir/Trisectrix_dir/trisectrix.html |access-date=2021-02-20}}</ref> The curve is one among a number of plane curve trisectrixes that includes the Conchoid of Nicomedes,<ref>{{cite web |title=Chonchoid of Nicomedes |url=http://people.math.harvard.edu/~knill/conchoid/exhibits/nicomedes/index.html |author=Oliver Knill |website=Harvard College Research Program project 2008 |access-date=2021-02-20}}</ref> the [[Tommaso Ceva#The Cycloid of Ceva|Cycloid of Ceva]],<ref>{{MathWorld |title=Cycloid of Ceva |urlname=CycloidofCeva.html}}</ref> [[Quadratrix of Hippias]], [[Trisectrix of Maclaurin]], and [[Tschirnhausen cubic]]. The limaçon trisectrix a special case of a [[sectrix of Maclaurin]].

== Specification and loop structure ==
The limaçon trisectrix specified as a [[polar equation]] is
:<math>r= a(1+2\cos\theta)</math>.<ref>{{cite web |title=Trisectrix |author=Xah Lee |url=http://xahlee.info/SpecialPlaneCurves_dir/Trisectrix_dir/trisectrix.html |access-date=2021-02-20}}</ref>
The constant <math>a</math> may be positive or negative.  The two curves with constants <math>a</math> and <math>-a</math> are [[reflection symmetry|reflections]] of each other across the line <math>\theta=\pi/2</math>. The period of <math>r= a(1+2\cos\theta)</math> is <math>2\pi</math> given the period of the [[sine wave|sinusoid]] <math>\cos\theta</math>.

The limaçon trisectrix is composed of two loops.
* The '''outer loop''' is defined when <math>1+2\cos\theta\ge0</math> on the polar angle interval <math>-2\pi/3 \le \theta \le 2\pi/3</math>, and is [[reflection symmetry|symmetric]] about the polar axis.  The point furthest from the pole on the outer loop has the coordinates <math>(3a,0)</math>.
* The '''inner loop''' is defined when <math>1+2\cos\theta\le0</math> on the polar angle interval <math>2\pi/3 \le \theta \le 4\pi/3</math>, and is symmetric about the polar axis.  The point furthest from the pole on the inner loop has the coordinates <math>(a,0)</math>, and on the polar axis, is one-third of the distance from the pole compared to the furthest point of the outer loop.
* The outer and inner loops intersect at the pole.

The curve can be specified in [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian coordinates]] as
:<math>a^2(x^2+y^2)= (x^2+y^2-2ax)^2</math>,

and parametric equations

:<math>x=(a+2a\cos\theta)\cos\theta=a(1+\cos\theta+\cos(2\theta))</math>,
:<math>y=(a+2a\cos\theta)\sin\theta=a(\sin\theta+\sin(2\theta))</math>.

=== Relationship with [[rose (mathematics)|rose]] curves ===
In polar coordinates, the shape of <math>r= a(1+2\cos\theta)</math> is the same as that of the rose <math>r = 2a\cos(\theta /3)</math>. Corresponding points of the rose are a distance <math>|a|</math> to the left of the limaçon's points when <math>a>0</math>, and <math>|a|</math> to the right when <math>a<0</math>.
As a rose, the curve has the structure of a single petal with two loops that is inscribed in the circle <math>r=2a</math> and is symmetric about the polar axis.

The inverse of this rose is a trisectrix since the inverse has the same shape as the [[trisectrix of Maclaurin]].

=== Relationship with the sectrix of Maclaurin ===
See the article [[Sectrix_of_Maclaurin#Lima%C3%A7on_trisectrix_and_rose |Sectrix of Maclaurin]] on the limaçon as an instance of the sectrix.

== Trisection properties ==
The outer and inner loops of the limaçon trisectrix have angle trisection properties.  Theoretically, an angle may be trisected using a method with either property, though practical considerations may limit use.

=== Outer loop trisectrix property ===
[[File:Limaçon trisectrix outer loop.png|thumb|300px|right|Angle trisection property of the (green) outer loop of the limaçon trisectrix <math>r=1+2\cos\theta</math>. The (blue) generating circle <math>r=2\cos\theta</math> is required to prove the trisection of <math>\angle{PMB}</math>. The (red) construction results in two angles, <math>\angle{QMP}</math> and <math>\angle{QPM}</math>, that have one-third the measure of <math>\angle{PMB}</math>; and one angle, <math>\angle{PAB}</math>, that has two-thirds the measure of <math>\angle{PMB}</math>.]]

The construction of the outer loop of <math>r=1+2\cos\theta</math> reveals its angle trisection properties.<ref>{{cite book |last=Yates |first=Robert C. |publication-date=1942 |title=The Trisection Problem |publisher=Franklin Press |location=Baton Rouge, Louisiana |edition=The National Council of Teachers of Mathematics |pages=23–25 |url=https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED058058.pdf}}</ref> The outer loop exists on the interval <math>-2\pi/3 \le \theta \le 2\pi/3</math>.  Here, we examine the trisectrix property of the portion of the outer loop above the polar axis, i.e., defined on the interval <math>0 \le \theta \le 2\pi/3</math>.

* First, note that polar equation <math>r=2\cos\theta</math> is a circle with radius <math>1</math>, center <math>M(1,0)</math> on the polar axis, and has a diameter that is tangent to the line <math>\theta=\pi/2</math> at the pole <math>A</math>.  Denote the diameter containing the pole as <math>\overline{AB}</math>, where <math>B</math> is at <math>(2,0)</math>.

* Second, consider any chord <math>\overline{AQ}</math> of the circle with the polar angle <math>\theta=\alpha</math>.  Since <math>\triangle{AQB}</math> is a right triangle, <math>AQ=2\cos\alpha</math>.  The corresponding point <math>P</math> on the outer loop has coordinates <math>(AQ+1,\alpha)</math>, where <math>0 < \alpha \le \pi</math>.

Given this construction, it is shown that <math>\angle{QMP}</math> and two other angles trisect <math>\angle{PMB}</math> as follows:

* <math>m\angle{QMB}=2\alpha</math>, as it is the [[central angle]] for <math>\widehat{QB}</math> on the circle <math>r=2\cos\theta</math>.

* The base angles of [[isosceles triangle]] <math>\triangle{AMQ}</math> measure <math>\alpha</math> – specifically, <math>m\angle{QAB}=m\angle{AQM}=\alpha</math>.

* The apex angle of isosceles triangle <math>\triangle{PQM}</math> is supplementary with <math>\angle{AQM}</math>, and so, <math>m\angle{PQM}=\pi-\alpha</math>.  Consequently the base angles, <math>\angle{QMP}</math> and <math>\angle{QPM}</math> measure <math>\alpha/2</math>.

* <math>m\angle{PMB}=m\angle{QMB}-m\angle{QMP}=2\alpha-\alpha/2=3\alpha/2</math>. Thus <math>\angle{PMB}</math> is trisected, since <math>m\angle{QMP}/m\angle{PMB}=1/3</math>.

* Note that also <math>m\angle{QPM}/m\angle{QMB}=1/3</math>, and <math>m\angle{PAB}/m\angle{QMB}=2/3</math>.

The upper half of the outer loop can trisect any central angle of <math>r=2\cos\theta</math> because <math>0<3\alpha/2<\pi</math> implies <math>0<\alpha<2\pi/3</math> which is in the domain of the outer loop.

=== Inner loop trisectrix property ===
[[File:Limicon_Trisectrix_inner_loop.png|thumb|300px|right|Angle trisection property of the (green) inner loop of the limaçon trisectrix <math>r=1+2\cos\theta</math>. Given a point <math>C</math> on the (blue) unit circle <math>r=1</math> centered at the pole <math>A</math> with <math>M</math> at <math>(1,0)</math>, where <math>\overline{CM}</math> (in red) intersects the inner loop at <math>P</math>, <math>\angle{PAM}</math> trisects <math>\angle{CAM}</math>. The (black) normal line to <math>\overleftrightarrow{CM}</math> is <math>\theta=\phi</math>, so <math>C</math> is at <math>(1,2\phi)</math>. The inner loop is redefined on the interval <math>0\le\theta\le\pi/3</math> as <math>r=-(1+2\cos(\theta+\pi))</math> because its native range is greater than <math>\pi</math> where its radial coordinates are non-positive.]]

The inner loop of the limaçon trisectrix has the desirable property that the trisection of an angle is internal to the angle being trisected.<ref>{{Cite EB1911 |wstitle= Trisectrix |volume= 27 | last= |first= |author-link= | page=292 |short=1}}</ref>  Here, we examine the inner loop of <math>r=1+2\cos\theta</math> that lies above the polar axis, which is defined on the polar angle interval <math>\pi \le \theta \le 4\pi/3</math>. The trisection property is that given a central angle that includes a point <math>C</math> lying on the [[unit circle]] with center at the pole, <math>r=1</math>, has a measure three times the measure of the polar angle of the point <math>P</math> at the intersection of chord <math>\overline{CM}</math> and the inner loop, where <math>M</math> is at <math>(1,0)</math>.

In Cartesian coordinates the equation of <math>\overleftrightarrow{CM}</math> is <math>y=k(x-1)</math>, where <math>k<0</math>, which is the polar equation

:<math>r=\frac{-k}{\sin\theta - k\cos\theta}=\frac{-k}{\cos(\theta-\phi)}=-k\sec(\theta-\phi)</math>, where <math>\tan\phi=\frac{1}{-k}</math> and <math>\phi=atan2(1,-k)</math>.  
(Note: [[atan2]](y,x) gives the polar angle of the Cartesian coordinate point (x,y).)

Since the normal line to <math>\overleftrightarrow{CM}</math> is <math>\theta=\phi</math>, it bisects the apex of isosceles triangle <math>\triangle{CAM}</math>, so <math>m\angle{CAM}=2\phi</math> and the polar coordinates of <math>C</math> is <math>(1,2\phi)</math>.

With respect to the limaçon, the range of polar angles <math>\pi \le \theta \le 4\pi/3</math> that defines the inner loop is problematic because the range of polar angles subject to trisection falls in the range <math>0\le\theta\le\pi</math>. Furthermore, on its native domain, the radial coordinates of the inner loop are non-positive.  The inner loop then is equivalently redefined within the polar angle range of interest and with non-negative radial coordinates as <math>r=-(1+2\cos(\theta+\pi))=-(1-2\cos\theta)</math>, where <math>-\cos(\theta+\pi)=\cos\theta</math>. Thus, the polar coordinate <math>\alpha</math> of <math>P</math> is determined by

:<math>-(1-2\cos\alpha)=\frac{-k}{\sin\alpha - k\cos\alpha}</math>
:<math>\rightarrow (\sin\alpha - k\cos\alpha)-2\cos\alpha\sin\alpha+2k\cos^2\alpha = k</math>
:<math>\rightarrow \cos(\alpha-\phi)-\sin(2\alpha)+2k (\frac{1+\cos(2\alpha)}{2})=k</math>
:<math>\rightarrow \cos(\alpha-\phi)-\sin(2\alpha)+k\cos(2\alpha)=0</math>
:<math>\rightarrow \cos(\alpha-\phi)=\cos(2\alpha-\phi)</math>.

The last equation has two solutions, the first being: <math>\alpha-\phi=2\alpha-\phi</math>, which results in <math>\alpha=0</math>, the polar axis, a line that intersects both curves but not at <math>C</math> on the unit circle.

The second solution is based on the identity <math>\cos(x) = \cos(-x)</math> which is expressed as
:<math>\alpha-\phi=\phi-2\alpha</math>, which implies <math>2\phi=3\alpha</math>,
and shows that <math>m\angle{CAM}=3(m\angle{PAM})</math> demonstrating the larger angle has been trisected.

The upper half of the inner loop can trisect any central angle of <math>r=1</math> because <math>0<3\alpha<\pi</math> implies <math>0<\alpha<\pi/3</math> which is in the domain of the redefined loop.

=== Line segment trisection property ===
The limaçon trisectrix <math>r=a(1+2\cos\theta)</math> trisects the [[line segment]] on the polar axis that serves as its axis of symmetry.  Since the outer loop extends to the point <math>(3a,0)</math> and the inner loop to the point <math>(a,0)</math>, the limaçon trisects the segment with endpoints at the pole (where the two loops intersect) and the point <math>(3a,0)</math>, where the total length of <math>3a</math> is three times the length running from the pole to the other end of the inner loop along the segment.

== Relationship with the trisectrix hyperbola ==

Given the limaçon trisectrix <math>r=1+2\cos\theta</math>, the inverse <math>r^{-1}</math> is the polar equation of a [[hyperbola]] with [[Eccentricity (mathematics)|eccentricity]] equal to 2, a curve that is a trisectrix. (See [[Hyperbola#Angle_trisection|Hyperbola - angle trisection]].)
